title: C++ Programming
tagline: Object-oriented design, templates, smart pointers, and high-performance engineering
description: Bridge low-level hardware control with high-level zero-cost abstractions. Master modern C++ (C++17/20), encapsulation, inheritance, dynamic polymorphism, operator overloading, templates, smart pointers, and the Standard Template Library (STL).

chapters.title: Chapter 1: Modern C++ Fundamentals & Streams
chapters.description: Stream-based I/O, namespaces, references, and modern type deduction with auto.

lessons.title: Streams, iostream, std::cout & Namespaces
lessons.summary: Learn type-safe stream insertion (<<), extraction (>>), the std namespace, and modern C++ compilation.
lessons.content:
### Evolution from C to Modern C++
Created by Bjarne Stroustrup in 1979 as 'C with Classes', C++ has evolved into an industrial powerhouse powering AAA game engines (Unreal Engine), high-frequency trading (HFT) platforms, web browsers (Chromium, V8), autonomous vehicles, and deep learning backends (PyTorch, TensorFlow).

### The Standard Streams: iostream vs stdio.h
Unlike C's `printf`, which relies on runtime string parsing and format specifiers, C++ uses type-safe I/O streams:
- `std::cout`: Standard character output stream.
- `<<` (Stream Insertion Operator): Inserts data into the stream; type resolution happens at compile time!
- `std::endl`: Inserts a newline character and flushes the output stream buffer.
- `std::cin`: Standard input stream using extraction (`>>`).

### Namespaces in C++
To prevent identifier collisions in massive multi-library codebases, C++ groups declarations within namespaces.
`std::` denotes symbols originating from the C++ Standard Library. While `using namespace std;` is often seen in tutorials, it pollutes the global scope and can cause ambiguous symbol conflicts in production code.

### The Modern C++ Philosophy
Modern C++ emphasizes **Zero-Cost Abstractions**: 'What you don't use, you don't pay for. And further: What you do use, you couldn't hand code any better.'

quizzes.question: What is the primary advantage of C++ std::cout over C's printf?
options: It requires fewer characters to type
It is completely type-safe and checked at compile time
It does not require including any header
It executes directly on the GPU
quizzes.explanation: Stream insertion (<<) is overloaded for each specific type at compile time, eliminating format string mismatch bugs present in printf.

practice.title: Double Value via Reference
practice.instructions: Implement `void doubleValue(int& val)` that doubles the parameter. Double a variable containing 14 and print the result.
practice.hint: val = val * 2 modifies the original variable directly through the reference.

quizzes.question: Can a C++ reference be uninitialized or set to nullptr?
options: Yes, using nullptr_t
No, a reference must always be initialized to a valid object when created
Only if declared as a const reference
Only in C++20 and above
quizzes.explanation: A reference in C++ is guaranteed to refer to an existing object. It cannot be null or uninitialized.

lessons.title: Type Deduction with auto & Modern Syntax
lessons.summary: Modern C++ features: auto type deduction, uniform initialization {}, and expressive coding.
lessons.content:
### Type Deduction with auto
Introduced in C++11, the `auto` keyword instructs the compiler to deduce the variable's type from its initialization expression at compile time:
```cpp
auto count = 10;          // deduced as int
auto ratio = 3.14159;     // deduced as double
auto name = "DevLearn";   // deduced as const char*
```
`auto` carries **zero runtime penalty** because deduction occurs entirely during compilation. It is invaluable when dealing with verbose template types like `std::vector<std::pair<std::string, int>>::const_iterator`.

### Uniform Initialization (Brace Initialization)
C++11 introduced `{}` initialization syntax for all types:
```cpp
int age{25};
int coords[]{10, 20, 30};
```
Brace initialization prevents narrowing conversions (e.g., initializing an `int` with a `double` raises a compile-time error).

practice.title: Calculate Area with Auto Deduction
practice.instructions: Declare auto width = 12 and auto height = 8. Calculate auto area = width * height, and print the result.
practice.hint: Use auto for all variable declarations.

quizzes.question: When does the C++ compiler resolve the type of an 'auto' variable?
options: At runtime using dynamic type reflection
At compile time with zero runtime overhead
During linking of the binary
When the variable is first printed
quizzes.explanation: Type deduction with auto occurs entirely at compile time. The resulting machine code is identical to declaring the type explicitly.

quizzes.question: What is the default visibility of members declared inside a C++ class?
options: public
private
protected
global
quizzes.explanation: In a C++ class, members default to private unless explicitly preceded by public: or protected:.

quizzes.question: What is the core principle of RAII (Resource Acquisition Is Initialization)?
options: All variables must be initialized to 0
Resources are acquired in the constructor and released automatically in the destructor upon scope exit
Classes must inherit from an abstract base class
Dynamic memory must be managed using malloc
quizzes.explanation: RAII ties resource lifecycle to object lifetime. When an object leaves scope, its destructor is called automatically, freeing resources safely.

private

lessons.title: Virtual Functions & Dynamic Polymorphism
lessons.summary: Late binding, virtual tables (vtable), the virtual keyword, override specifier, and pure virtual abstract classes.
lessons.content:
### Static vs Dynamic Binding
By default, C++ binds function calls at compile time (**early/static binding**) based on the pointer/reference type, NOT the actual object type. To achieve runtime polymorphism (**late/dynamic binding**), member functions must be marked `virtual`.

### How the Virtual Table (vtable) Works
When a class contains at least one virtual function:
1. The compiler constructs a hidden table of function pointers called the **vtable** for that class.
2. Every object of that class contains an invisible pointer (`vptr`) pointing to the vtable.
3. At runtime, calling a virtual method dereferences the `vptr` and invokes the actual derived implementation.

### Pure Virtual Functions & Abstract Interfaces
A function with `= 0` is pure virtual. A class with at least one pure virtual function is **abstract** and cannot be instantiated directly:
```cpp
class Shape {
public:
    virtual void draw() = 0; // Pure virtual
    virtual ~Shape() = default; // Essential virtual destructor!
};
```

practice.title: Implement Polymorphic Logger
practice.instructions: Create a BaseLogger with virtual void log(), and ConsoleLogger that overrides log() to print 'Log: Console Dispatched'.
practice.hint: Mark BaseLogger method with virtual, and ConsoleLogger with override.

quizzes.question: Why is it mandatory for polymorphic base classes to declare a virtual destructor?
options: To improve program startup performance
To ensure derived class destructors are executed when deleting via a base class pointer, preventing resource leaks
Because compilers refuse to build without it
To convert the class into a singleton
quizzes.explanation: If a base class destructor is not virtual, calling delete on a base pointer to a derived object causes undefined behavior and fails to call the derived destructor.

chapters.title: Chapter 4: Templates & Generic Programming
chapters.description: Function templates, class templates, and type-independent generic algorithms.

lessons.title: Function & Class Templates
lessons.summary: Write generic, type-agnostic algorithms that compile to highly optimized machine code for any data type.
lessons.content:
### What are Templates?
Templates enable generic programming by allowing functions and classes to operate with parameterized types. Instead of writing duplicate functions for `int`, `float`, and `double`, you define a single template:
```cpp
template <typename T>
T getMax(T a, T b) {
    return (a > b) ? a : b;
}
```

### Template Instantiation
When the compiler encounters `getMax(10, 20)`, it instantiates an `int` version of the function at compile time. When it encounters `getMax(3.5, 1.2)`, it generates a `double` version.
- **Zero Runtime Overhead**: Templates produce specialized machine code equivalent to hand-written functions.
- **Header Inclusion**: Because the compiler generates code during compilation, template definitions must reside in header files (`.hpp` or `.h`), not `.cpp` files.

practice.title: Build a Generic Multiply Template
practice.instructions: Create a template `T multiply(T a, T b)` that returns a * b. Test with values 6 and 7.
practice.hint: Use template <typename T> T multiply(T a, T b) { return a * b; }

quizzes.question: When does template instantiation take place in C++?
options: At compile time when the template is invoked with concrete types
At runtime by an interpreter
During OS executable loading
Only in debug mode
quizzes.explanation: C++ templates are instantiated by the compiler at compile time, creating concrete implementations for each type used.

chapters.title: Chapter 5: Modern Memory & Smart Pointers
chapters.description: Eliminate raw pointers and leaks with std::unique_ptr and std::shared_ptr.

lessons.title: Smart Pointers: std::unique_ptr & std::shared_ptr
lessons.summary: Automatic memory management in modern C++ (<memory>), exclusive ownership vs shared reference counting.
lessons.content:
### The Death of Raw 'new' and 'delete'
In legacy C++, forgetting `delete` caused memory leaks, while calling `delete` twice caused undefined behavior. Modern C++ solves this completely using **Smart Pointers** that implement RAII:

### 1. `std::unique_ptr<T>` (Exclusive Ownership)
- Represents strict, single ownership of a heap resource.
- Cannot be copied (copy constructor is deleted), only moved (`std::move`).
- When the `unique_ptr` goes out of scope, it deletes the managed object automatically.
- **Zero Overhead**: Has the exact same memory footprint and performance as a raw pointer!
```cpp
auto ptr = std::make_unique<Resource>(args);
```

### 2. `std::shared_ptr<T>` (Shared Ownership)
- Multiple `shared_ptr` instances share ownership of an object.
- Maintains an atomic **reference counter** in a control block.
- When the reference counter drops to zero, the object is deallocated.

quizzes.question: Can a std::unique_ptr be copied to another std::unique_ptr using assignment (=)?
options: Yes, it increments the reference counter
No, unique_ptr represents exclusive ownership; it can only be moved, not copied
Yes, but only in C++20
Only if the target is null
quizzes.explanation: std::unique_ptr has a deleted copy constructor to enforce unique ownership. It can only be transferred using move semantics.

lessons.title: STL Containers: std::vector & Dynamic Storage
lessons.summary: Dynamic resizing arrays with std::vector, push_back, size, capacity, and contiguous cache-friendly storage.
lessons.content:
### Why std::vector is C++'s Default Container
Bjarne Stroustrup famously stated: 'By default, use vector when you need a container.'
`std::vector` is a contiguous dynamic array that manages its own memory:
1. **Contiguous Memory**: Elements are stored sequentially in memory, maximizing CPU cache line hits and traversal speed.
2. **Automatic Growth**: When capacity is exceeded, it allocates a new larger buffer (typically 1.5x or 2x) and moves existing elements.
3. **Random Access**: O(1) constant-time element lookup by index `v[i]`.

### Key Vector Operations
- `v.push_back(val)`: Appends an element to the end.
- `v.size()`: Returns the number of elements currently stored.
- `v.capacity()`: Returns the allocated storage space before a re-allocation is triggered.
- `v.clear()`: Destroys all elements.
lessons.expectedOutput:
Vector Container Initialized
Appended: 10, 20, 30
Vector Size: 3
Elements Traversed Successfully

practice.title: Simulate Dynamic List Storage

quizzes.question: What is the time complexity of accessing an arbitrary element in std::vector by index?
options: O(N)
O(log N)
O(1) Constant Time
quizzes.explanation: Because std::vector stores data in contiguous memory, indexing v[i] performs simple pointer arithmetic, executing in O(1) constant time.
